CMP-7.rationale: Environmental planners prepare the restoration and monitoring plan (creation methods, monitoring, funding, long-term management, agency reporting) implemented concurrently with construction; deliverable is the plan.

CMP-8.name: Create or Acquire and Protect Vernal Pool Complex
CMP-8.quote: Vernal pool complex will be created or acquired and permanently protected to compensate for project impacts to ensure no significant loss of vernal pool complex functions and values. In addition, vernal pool complex will be acquired and permanently protected to further compensate for project impacts.
CMP-8.rationale: Mitigation specialists create, acquire, and permanently protect vernal pool complex to offset project impacts; deliverable is protected compensatory acreage.

CMP-8.name: Develop Restoration and Monitoring Plan for Vernal Pool Complex
CMP-8.quote: A restoration and monitoring plan will be developed and implemented concurrently with project construction. The plan will describe how vernal pool complex will be created and monitored, including funding mechanisms and appropriate long-term management measures, and agency reporting requirements.
CMP-8.rationale: Environmental planners prepare the restoration and monitoring plan (creation methods, monitoring, funding, long-term management, agency reporting) implemented concurrently with construction; deliverable is the plan.

CMP-9.name: Restore and Protect Plant Habitat at 2:1 Ratio
CMP-9.quote: Mitigation habitat will consist of existing, off-site suitable habitat acquired in fee, through conservation easements, or from a certified conservation bank. At least 2 acres of habitat will be restored and protected for every 1 acre that would be lost.
CMP-9.rationale: Mitigation specialists acquire/restore off-site suitable habitat; the 2:1 acreage ratio is a distinct measurable compliance check.

CMP-9.name: Reestablish Plants Using Locally Sourced Propagules
CMP-9.quote: Reestablishing a plant species into suitable, historically supported habitat may include actions such as transplanting, propagation of seed, weed abatement, restoration of microtopography, and siting near existing occurrences. If propagation of seed is used, it will be conducted with consideration of maintenance of genetic diversity. Any propagation material would be sourced from the population affected by the project.
CMP-9.rationale: Restoration crews carry out reestablishment actions (transplanting, seed propagation, weed abatement) with propagules sourced from the affected population; applies where reestablishment is used.

CMP-9.name: Develop Special-Status Plant Restoration and Monitoring Plan
CMP-9.quote: A restoration and monitoring plan will be developed and implemented concurrently with project construction. The plan will include success criteria, specify the length of the monitoring period, and contain assurances of implementation, monitoring, and maintenance.
CMP-9.rationale: Environmental planners prepare the plan with success criteria, monitoring period, and implementation assurances; deliverable is the plan.

CMP-9.name: Site Restored Plant Habitat Near Extant Populations
CMP-9.quote: Restored special-status plant habitat will be carried out concurrently with sensitive natural community mitigation and sited in areas near extant populations of the affected species that could provide vegetative or seed propagules. Restored habitat will be sited in locations subject to CDFW approval.
CMP-9.rationale: Permitting staff obtain CDFW approval of restoration site locations near extant populations; deliverable is CDFW site approval.

CMP-9.name: Monitor Plant Mitigation Habitat Annually
CMP-9.quote: The mitigation habitat will be monitored annually to verify that the habitat suitability is maintained.
CMP-9.rationale: Field monitors verify habitat suitability each year; recurring annual monitoring.

CMP-9.name: Submit Annual Plant Mitigation Monitoring Reports to CDFW
CMP-9.quote: Annual monitoring reports will be submitted to CDFW for review and determination that the project remains in compliance with the mitigation.
CMP-9.rationale: Compliance staff submit annual monitoring reports to CDFW; deliverable is each annual report.

CMP-10.name: Restore Mason’s Lilaeopsis Habitat Within Tidal Mitigation
CMP-10.quote: Impacts on Mason’s lilaeopsis habitat will be offset through restoration of suitable habitat. Restored Mason’s lilaeopsis habitat will be a subset of tidal restoration mitigation and sited in areas near extant populations of Mason’s lilaeopsis that could provide vegetative or seed propagules.
CMP-10.rationale: Restoration crews restore suitable habitat as a subset of tidal restoration, sited near extant populations.

CMP-10.name: Obtain CDFW Approval of Lilaeopsis Restoration Sites
CMP-10.quote: Restored habitat will be sited in locations subject to CDFW approval.
CMP-10.rationale: Permitting staff secure CDFW approval of restoration locations; deliverable is the approval.

CMP-11.name: Preserve and Create Vernal Pool Shrimp Habitat
CMP-11.quote: Compensatory mitigation for vernal pool fairy shrimp and vernal pool tadpole shrimp habitat directly or indirectly affected will consist of the preservation of habitat and the creation of habitat at either a USFWS-approved mitigation bank or at a non-bank site approved by USFWS supporting habitat for vernal pool fairy shrimp and vernal pool tadpole shrimp.
CMP-11.rationale: Mitigation specialists preserve and create fairy/tadpole shrimp habitat at a USFWS-approved bank or approved non-bank site. Shrimp species are not in the project or global species lists, so none tagged.

CMP-12.name: Offset Permanent Riparian Loss with Creation and Enhancement
CMP-12.quote: the permanent loss of suitable riparian habitat will be offset with riparian creation and enhancement consistent with the restoration guidance in the Framework.
CMP-12.rationale: Mitigation specialists offset permanent riparian habitat loss following USFWS 2017 VELB Framework guidance.

CMP-12.name: Restore Temporarily Affected Areas On-Site
CMP-12.quote: All temporarily affected areas will be restored on-site and where on-site restoration is not possible the habitat will be replaced.
CMP-12.rationale: Restoration crews restore each temporarily affected area on-site, replacing habitat where on-site restoration is not possible.

CMP-12.name: Transplant Affected Elderberry Shrubs to CMP Mitigation Areas
CMP-12.quote: All elderberry shrubs that are 1 inch or more in diameter at ground level in riparian habitat that will be affected will be transplanted to mitigation areas identified in the CMP. All elderberry shrubs in non-riparian areas that will be affected will be transplanted to mitigation areas identified in the CMP if they contain exit holes.
CMP-12.rationale: Restoration crews transplant qualifying elderberry shrubs (size/exit-hole thresholds) before they are affected; deliverable is transplant records.

CMP-12.name: Monitor and Adaptively Manage Transplanted Elderberry Shrubs
CMP-12.quote: All transplanted shrubs will be monitored and adaptively managed for survivorship as part of the site-specific maintenance and management plan and the monitoring and adaptive management plan as described in Section 3F.7 and Section 3F.6.4, Adaptive Management, respectively.
CMP-12.rationale: Field monitors track survivorship of transplanted shrubs under the maintenance/adaptive management plans.

CMP-13.name: Protect CTS Habitat in Bank or Site Protection Instrument
CMP-13.quote: To the extent possible, California tiger salamander habitat protection will be located in a mitigation bank (with a service area that overlaps with the impact area) or other site protection instrument in the geographically appropriate Recovery management unit of the Central Valley, which is identified in USFWS’s Plan for the Central California Distinct Population Segment of the California Tiger Salamander (Ambystoma californiense) (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2017b).
CMP-13.rationale: Mitigation specialists secure CTS habitat protection in a mitigation bank or other site protection instrument within the appropriate recovery unit.

CMP-13.name: Prioritize CTS Land Acquisition by Habitat Criteria
CMP-13.quote: If a mitigation bank is not used, land acquisition for California tiger salamander will be prioritized based on the following characteristics. Large contiguous landscapes that consist of grasslands, vernal pool complex,  and alkali seasonal wetland complex and encompass the range of vegetation, hydrologic, and soil conditions that characterize these communities. Lands that maintain connectivity with protected grassland, vernal pool  complex, and alkali seasonal wetland complex landscapes near proposed construction sites, including connectivity with lands that have been protected or may be protected in the future under the East Contra Costa County Habitat Conservation Plan/Natural Community Conservation Plan. Grasslands containing stock ponds and other aquatic features that provide  aquatic breeding habitat for California tiger salamander. Adjacent or connected to occupied California tiger salamander upland or  aquatic habitat.
CMP-13.rationale: Site selection applying listed landscape, connectivity, and breeding-habitat criteria; only triggered if a mitigation bank is not used.

CMP-14.name: Protect California Red-Legged Frog Habitat in Recovery Area
CMP-14.quote: To mitigate for the loss of California red-legged frog aquatic and upland habitat, DWR will protect suitable habitat. California red-legged frog aquatic breeding and upland habitat will be prioritized for protection within the East San Francisco Bay Recovery Plan for the California Red-Legged core recovery area as described in the Frog (Rana aurora draytonii) (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2002), at a location subject to USFWS approval.
CMP-14.rationale: Mitigation specialists protect suitable CRLF breeding and upland habitat, prioritized in the East SF Bay core recovery area at a USFWS-approved location. CRLF not in species lists.

CMP-14.name: Manage Protected CRLF Lands in Perpetuity
CMP-14.quote: All lands protected and restored for compensation of effects on California red-legged frog habitat will be protected and managed in perpetuity.
CMP-14.rationale: Long-term land management of protected and restored CRLF lands; ongoing obligation.

CMP-14.name: Prioritize CRLF Land Acquisition by Connectivity Criteria
CMP-14.quote: Land acquisition for California red-legged frog habitat management lands will be prioritized based on the following characteristics. Lands that connect with existing protected grassland, vernal pool complex,  and alkali seasonal wetland complex landscapes, including those in the East San Francisco Bay core recovery area for California red-legged frog.
CMP-14.rationale: Site selection applying the connectivity criteria to acquisition lands.

CMP-15.name: Compensate for Unavoidable Giant Garter Snake Habitat Loss
CMP-15.quote: Where identified and delineated giant garter snake habitat cannot be avoided, compensation for the loss of the habitat will occur for aquatic and upland habitat, with in-kind habitat type compensation.
CMP-15.rationale: Mitigation specialists provide in-kind aquatic and upland compensation where habitat cannot be avoided (conditional).

CMP-15.name: Site GGS Mitigation by Buffer and Distance Criteria
CMP-15.quote: Giant garter snake upland mitigation will be placed and protected adjacent to  aquatic habitat protected for giant garter snake. The upland habitat will not exceed 200 feet from protected aquatic habitat (unless research shows a larger distance is appropriate and USFWS and CDFW agree). Incidental injury or mortality of giant garter snakes within protected and  restored habitat will be avoided and minimized by establishing 200-foot buffers between protected giant garter snake habitat and roads (other than those roads primarily used to support adjacent cultivated lands and levees). Protected and restored giant garter snake habitat will be at least 2,500 feet  from urban areas or areas zoned for urban development. Characteristics of restored and protected habitat may change from the above  descriptors if new information and best available science indicate greater benefits as agreed upon by USFWS and CDFW.
CMP-15.rationale: Siting criteria with measurable thresholds (upland within 200 ft, 200-ft road buffers, 2,500 ft from urban areas); verified at site selection.

CMP-15.name: Design Nontidal Marsh Mitigation to GGS Criteria
CMP-15.quote: Siting and design requirements for the restoration and protection of giant garter snake nontidal wetland habitat are listed below. For in-kind mitigation sites, the aquatic and upland habitat quality, character,  and location must be of equal or greater value than the habitat quality that was lost. Conservation mitigation sites will be characterized as nontidal marsh and will  meet the following design criteria. Restored nontidal marsh will be characterized by sufficient water during  the giant garter snake’s active summer season (May 1–October 1) to supply constant, reliable cover and sources of food such as small fish and amphibians. Restored nontidal marsh will consist of still or slow-flowing water over a  substrate composed of soil, silt, or mud characteristic of those observed in marshes, sloughs, or irrigation canals. Restoration designs will not create large areas of deep, perennial open  water that would support nonnative predatory fish. The restored marsh will be characterized by a heterogeneous topography providing a range of depths and vegetation profiles consisting of emergent, herbaceous aquatic vegetation that will provide suitable foraging habitat and refuge from predators. Aquatic margins or shorelines will transition to uplands consisting of  grassy banks, with the dense grassy understory required for sheltering. These margins will consist of approximately 200 feet of high ground or upland habitat above the annual high-water mark to provide cover and refugia from floodwaters during the dormant winter season. The upland habitat will have ample exposure to sunlight to facilitate giant  garter snake thermoregulation and will be characterized by low vegetation, bankside burrows, holes, and crevices providing critical shelter for snakes throughout the day. All giant garter snake upland and aquatic habitat will be established at least 2,500 feet from urban areas or areas zoned for urban development.
CMP-15.rationale: Engineers design restored nontidal marsh to listed hydrology, topography, vegetation, and upland-margin criteria; deliverable is a compliant restoration design.

CMP-15.name: Design Tidal GGS Habitat Restoration with Terrestrial Refuge
CMP-15.quote: The loss of tidal aquatic habitat for giant garter snake may be mitigated  through restoration of tidal habitat with a design that provides equal or greater habitat value for the species as agreed upon by USFWS and CDFW. Topography of the restored wetlands will be designed to provide adjacent terrestrial refuge persisting above the high-water mark. Terrestrial features will be sited within 200 feet of aquatic foraging areas at all tide levels, with slopes and grading designed to avoid exposing largely denuded intertidal mud flats during low tide.
CMP-15.rationale: Engineers design tidal restoration with refuge above high water within 200 ft of foraging areas; applies only if tidal loss is mitigated through tidal restoration.

CMP-16.name: Create or Restore Riparian Habitat to Offset Yellow-Billed Cuckoo Loss
CMP-16.quote: DWR will offset the loss of western yellow-billed cuckoo habitat through the creation or restoration of riparian habitat in the study area.
CMP-16.rationale: Restoration crews create or restore riparian habitat in the study area to offset Yellow-Billed Cuckoo habitat loss.

CMP-16.name: Develop Riparian Restoration Plan for USFWS Approval
CMP-16.quote: DWR will develop a riparian restoration plan that will identify the location and methods for riparian creation or restoration, and this plan will be subject to USFWS approval.
CMP-16.rationale: Environmental planners prepare a restoration plan identifying location and methods, subject to USFWS approval; deliverable is the approved plan.

CMP-17.name: Create or Restore Tidal Wetland Habitat to Offset Black Rail Loss
CMP-17.quote: DWR will offset the loss of California black rail habitat through the creation or restoration of tidal emergent wetland habitat in the study area.
CMP-17.rationale: Restoration crews create or restore tidal wetland habitat in the study area to offset Black Rail habitat loss.

CMP-17.name: Develop Tidal Wetland Restoration Plan for CDFW Approval
CMP-17.quote: DWR will develop a restoration plan that will identify the location and methods for tidal emergent wetland creation or restoration, and this plan will be subject to CDFW approval.
CMP-17.rationale: Environmental planners prepare a restoration plan identifying location and methods, subject to CDFW approval; deliverable is the approved plan.

CMP-18a.name: Create Sandhill Crane Roosting Habitat in 40-Acre Patches
CMP-18a.quote: Create suitable sandhill crane roosting habitat in minimum patch sizes of 40 acres within the Greater Sandhill Crane Winter Use Area with consideration of sea level rise and local seasonal flood events.
CMP-18a.rationale: Restoration crews create roosting habitat meeting the 40-acre minimum patch size within the Winter Use Area.

CMP-18a.name: Obtain CDFW Approval of Roosting Habitat Location
CMP-18a.quote: Roosting habitat may be created on Bouldin Island or in suitable lands that provide connectivity between the Stone Lakes National Wildlife Refuge boundary and the Cosumnes River Preserve, subject to CDFW approval.
CMP-18a.rationale: Permitting staff obtain CDFW approval of the roosting habitat location; deliverable is the approval.

CMP-18b.name: Protect Sandhill Crane Foraging Habitat, 80% Very High Value
CMP-18b.quote: Protect high- to very high-value foraging habitat for greater sandhill crane (corn, rice, wheat, and freshwater emergent wetlands), with at least 80% maintained in very high-value types (corn and rice) in any given year, subject to CDFW approval.
CMP-18b.rationale: Mitigation land managers protect foraging habitat and maintain at least 80% in corn/rice each year; annual crop-mix compliance check.

CMP-18b.name: Site Crane Foraging Habitat Near Roosts in 160-Acre Patches
CMP-18b.quote: This foraging habitat will be within 2 miles of new project roost sites and will consider sea level rise and local seasonal flood events, and the location of foraging habitat loss. The patch size of protected cultivated lands will be at least 160 acres.
CMP-18b.rationale: Site selection with measurable thresholds (within 2 miles of roosts, 160-acre minimum patches, sea-level-rise consideration).

CMP-19a.name: Restore and Protect Swainson’s Hawk Nesting Habitat
CMP-19a.quote: Swainson’s hawk nesting habitat will be restored and protected at a location agreed upon in writing by CDFW at that time.
CMP-19a.rationale: Mitigation specialists restore and protect nesting habitat at a CDFW-agreed location.

CMP-19a.name: Determine Affected Nest Sites Using 125-Acre Grid
CMP-19a.quote: To determine the number of affected suitable nest sites, a grid of 125-acre blocks will be placed over each component of project footprint in which trees are to be removed. The grid will be overlain in a manner that places the most complete squares of the grid in the project footprint (i.e., the grid will be adjusted so that, to the extent possible, entire squares rather than portions of squares will overlap with the project footprint).
CMP-19a.rationale: Desk GIS analysis overlaying 125-acre grid on each component footprint with tree removal; deliverable is the count of affected nest sites.

CMP-19a.name: Establish Replacement Swainson’s Hawk Nest Sites
CMP-19a.quote: Nest Site Replacement In addition to the compensatory mitigation listed above, DWR will compensate for the temporal loss of suitable Swainson’s hawk nest sites (defined as a 125-acre area where more than 50% of suitable nest trees [20 feet or taller] within the 125- acre block are removed). To establish a new nest site, DWR will transplant five mature suitable nest trees (at least 20 feet tall) and 15 five-gallon-container-sized suitable nest trees to a location specified in a Vegetation Restoration Plan that is within preserved mitigation lands and approved in writing by CDFW.
CMP-19a.rationale: Restoration crews transplant 5 mature trees and 15 saplings per affected nest site per a CDFW-approved Vegetation Restoration Plan; triggered by nest-site loss.

CMP-19a.name: Plant Five Native Trees per Suitable Nest Tree Removed
CMP-19a.quote: For each suitable nest tree removed for the project, DWR will plant five native trees (5-gallon container size) suitable for Swainson’s hawk nesting to replace lost suitable nest trees at sites within 3 miles of conserved foraging habitat.
CMP-19a.rationale: Measurable 5:1 replacement ratio for each nest tree removed; distinct compliance check.

CMP-19a.name: Monitor Replacement Nest Trees for 80% Survival
CMP-19a.quote: DWR will monitor and maintain all replacement nest trees (mature trees and saplings) for a period of 10 years to assure survival and appropriate growth and development. Success will be measured as an 80% survival rate of mature trees and saplings at 5 and 10 years after planting. After the first 10 years, DWR will monitor replacement nest trees every 5 years to verify their continued survival and growth.
CMP-19a.rationale: Field monitors track survival for 10 years (80% at years 5 and 10) then every 5 years.

CMP-19a.name: Replace Failed Trees and Irrigate Replacement Nest Trees
CMP-19a.quote: For every tree lost during the 10-year time period, DWR will immediately plant a replacement tree upon the detection of failure. DWR will provide all necessary maintenance (i.e., fertilizing, irrigation) to ensure successful establishment. DWR will irrigate trees for a minimum of 5 years after planting, and then gradually wean the trees off the irrigation during a period of approximately 2 years. If larger stock is planted, DWR may reduce the number of years of irrigation accordingly.
CMP-19a.rationale: Restoration crews replant failures, fertilize, and irrigate for at least 5 years with a ~2-year wean.

CMP-19a.name: Coordinate with CDFW if Nest Tree Success Criteria Fail
CMP-19a.quote: If the 80% establishment success criteria cannot be met, DWR will coordinate with CDFW to determine additional measures.
CMP-19a.rationale: Regulatory staff consult CDFW on additional measures only if the 80% success criterion is not met.

CMP-19b.name: Protect Swainson’s Hawk Foraging Habitat Meeting Siting Criteria
CMP-19b.quote: Swainson’s hawk foraging habitat will be protected at locations subject to CDFW approval and will meet the following criteria. Foraging habitat will be protected within 3 miles of a known Swainson’s hawk  nest tree and within 50 miles of the project footprint. Where feasible, protected foraging habitat will have land surface elevations  equal to or greater than -1 foot NAVD88 to minimize the risk of flooding and loss of suitable habitat due to future sea level rise. Where protected foraging habitat is located at elevations lower than -1 foot NAVD88, DWR will ensure that levees are maintained around protected habitat. Individual patches of foraging habitat will be at least 40 acres in size.
CMP-19b.rationale: Mitigation specialists protect CDFW-approved foraging habitat within 3 miles of a nest and 50 miles of the footprint, 40-acre patches, elevation/levee criteria.

CMP-19b.name: Establish Hedgerows at 400 Linear Feet per 100 Acres
CMP-19b.quote: Swainson’s hawk prey populations will be supported by establishing 20- to  30-foot-wide hedgerows along field borders and roadsides at a minimum rate of 400 linear feet per 100 acres of protected cultivated lands.
CMP-19b.rationale: Restoration crews plant 20–30 ft hedgerows at a measurable minimum rate.

CMP-19b.name: Prohibit Rodenticide Use on Compensation Lands
CMP-19b.quote: The use of rodenticide will be prohibited on compensation lands to mitigate  for Swainson’s hawk foraging habitat.
CMP-19b.rationale: Land managers observe an ongoing prohibition; distinct prohibition compliance check.

CMP-19b.name: Provide Mitigation Acres for All Lost Foraging Habitat Classes
CMP-19b.quote: Mitigation acres will be provided for all acres of habitat lost in the very high,  high, medium, and low value classes (see Table 13B.72-1 in Appendix 13B, Species Accounts, Habitat Value Categories, Section 13B.72.5.3, for definitions of Swainson’s hawk foraging habitat value). Lands that are fallowed in any given season or year will be assigned the same habitat value as the dominant crop type on those lands.
CMP-19b.rationale: Desk calculation of required mitigation acreage by habitat value class (fallowed land assigned dominant crop value).

CMP-19b.name: Maintain Mitigation Lands in Required Crop Value Mix
CMP-19b.quote: Cultivated lands will be maintained in nonpermanent crop types as follows: At least 37.5% of Swainson’s hawk mitigation lands will be in very high–  value foraging habitat on an annual basis. The amount of very high–value habitat used for mitigation will increase  to at least the amount lost to project activities, if it is more than 37.5% of the total affected Swainson’s hawk foraging habitat. At least 25% of Swainson’s hawk mitigation lands will be in high-value  foraging habitat and other grasslands managed for Swainson’s hawk use on an annual basis. At least 22.5% of Swainson’s hawk mitigation lands will be in medium-  value foraging habitat. No more than 15% of Swainson’s hawk mitigation lands will be in low-  value foraging habitat on an annual basis. No Swainson’s hawk mitigation lands will be placed on a site that does not have one of the above-listed assigned habitat values (or their equivalent).
CMP-19b.rationale: Annual compliance with percentage thresholds per habitat value class (≥37.5% very high, ≥25% high, ≥22.5% medium, ≤15% low).

CMP-20.name: Protect Burrowing Owl Habitat per CDFG Staff Report
CMP-20.quote: Suitable burrowing owl habitat will be protected, using the best practices described in the Staff Report on Burrowing Owl Mitigation (California Department of Fish and Game 2012:11–14).
CMP-20.rationale: Mitigation specialists protect suitable habitat using Staff Report best practices where the site is considered occupied. Burrowing owl not in species lists.

CMP-20.name: Consult CDFW on Mitigation if Take or Burrow Relocation
CMP-20.quote: If construction activities result in take or if an active burrow must be relocated, as appropriate, DWR will consult with CDFW to develop effective mitigation alternatives.
CMP-20.rationale: Regulatory staff consult CDFW only if take occurs or an active burrow must be relocated.

CMP-21.name: Create or Restore Riparian Habitat to Offset Least Bell’s Vireo Loss
CMP-21.quote: DWR will offset the loss of least Bell’s vireo habitat through the creation or restoration of riparian habitat in the study area.
CMP-21.rationale: Restoration crews create or restore riparian habitat in the study area to offset Least Bell’s Vireo habitat loss.

CMP-21.name: Develop Riparian Restoration Plan for USFWS Approval
CMP-21.quote: DWR will develop a riparian restoration plan that will identify the location and methods for riparian creation or restoration, and this plan will be subject to USFWS approval.
CMP-21.rationale: Environmental planners prepare a restoration plan identifying location and methods, subject to USFWS approval; deliverable is the approved plan.

CMP-22a.name: Protect or Restore Tricolored Blackbird Nesting Habitat
CMP-22a.quote: To offset the loss of occupied tricolored blackbird nesting habitat, or previously occupied tricolored blackbird colonies (colonies that have been active within the past 15 years) will be permanently protected or restored and managed at a location subject to CDFW approval, and within 5 miles of the nearest breeding colony observed within the past 15 years if possible. Protected or restored nesting habitat will be managed to provide young, lush stands of bulrush/cattail emergent vegetation and prevent vegetation senescence; or other nesting substrate determined to be location and use appropriate and agreed to by CDFW.
CMP-22a.rationale: Mitigation specialists protect/restore nesting habitat within 5 miles of a colony at a CDFW-approved location, managed for young emergent stands.

CMP-22a.name: Prioritize Nesting Habitat Sites by Habitat Characteristics
CMP-22a.quote: Nesting habitat protection or restoration will be prioritized based on the following characteristics. Alternative nesting habitat can be considered based on best available science (e.g., protection of upland tricolored blackbird nesting habitat including blackberries or some of the other upland vegetation species frequently used by tricolored blackbirds for nesting) and CDFW approval. Occupied or recently occupied (i.e., within the last 15 years) stands of  bulrush/cattail emergent vegetation. Wetland marsh habitat that contains standing water to a depth of  approximately 1 foot in most years from late January through late July to encourage dense development of cattail and bulrush vegetation and to provide protection from predators until nesting is completed; and that is within 6 kilometers of high- or very high–quality foraging habitat. High or very high–quality breeding season foraging habitat includes native pasture, nonirrigated native pasture, annual grassland, vernal pool grassland, alkali grassland, unsprayed alfalfa, unsprayed sunflower, and unsprayed mixed alfalfa, sunflower, alfalfa, mixed alfalfa, mixed pasture, and induced high water table native pasture, and nonirrigated mixed pasture, and dairies, as Breeding Foraging Habitat described in Appendix 13B, Section 13B.85.5.3, Value Categories, Table 13B.85-1.
CMP-22a.rationale: Site selection applying listed criteria (occupied stands, water depth, proximity to high-value foraging).

CMP-22a.name: Manage Bulrush/Cattail Stands Every 2 to 5 Years
CMP-22a.quote: Management and enhancement of tricolored blackbird nesting habitat will be  consistent with the recommendations provided by Kyle (2011). The following criteria will guide site selection and management of emergent wetland habitat to benefit tricolored blackbird. Burn, mow, or graze bulrush/cattail vegetation every 2 to 5 years, or an  appropriate interval necessary and agreed to by CDFW to remove dead growth and encourage the development of new vegetative structure. Maintain large continuous stands of bulrush/cattail that are at least 30 to 45  feet wide to provide adequate space for breeding as well as protection from predators.
CMP-22a.rationale: Land managers burn, mow, or graze on a 2–5 year cycle and maintain 30–45 ft wide stands per Kyle (2011).

CMP-22a.name: Establish Seasonal Buffers Around Restored Nesting Habitat
CMP-22a.quote: Establish seasonal buffer zones (consistent with buffers described in Chapter 13, Mitigation Measure BIO-33) around restored tricolored blackbird nesting habitat to reduce disturbance and improve foraging habitat for tricolored blackbirds.
CMP-22a.rationale: Protective buffers consistent with BIO-33 to reduce disturbance; distinct avoidance measure.

CMP-22a.name: Establish Nesting Substrate Along Ditches and Canals
CMP-22a.quote: Where conditions permit, stands of emergent vegetation, native blackberry, or other native vegetation will be established along ditches and canals to provide suitable nesting substrate for tricolored blackbird. These stands will be located near foraging sites and DWR will prioritize sites located within the dispersal range of existing tricolored blackbird nesting colonies.
CMP-22a.rationale: Restoration crews plant nesting substrate along ditches and canals where conditions permit.

CMP-22b.name: Protect TRBL Breeding Foraging Habitat Within 6 km of Nesting
CMP-22b.quote: To support protected or restored tricolored blackbird nesting habitat, or to offset the loss of breeding foraging habitat (i.e., foraging habitat used during the breeding season), breeding foraging habitat will be protected using a site protection Site Protection Instruments. instrument as described in Section 3F.4.2.2, Breeding foraging habitat will be protected at a location subject to CDFW approval within 6 kilometers of (1) protected or restored nesting habitat that is managed for tricolored blackbird or (2) a recently or historically (to encourage recolonization) occupied tricolored blackbird nesting habitat.
CMP-22b.rationale: Mitigation specialists protect breeding foraging habitat by site protection instrument at a CDFW-approved location within 6 km of nesting habitat.

CMP-22b.name: Maintain 50% of Foraging Lands in High-Value Crops Annually
CMP-22b.quote: To allow for normal crop rotation, 50% of land protected as tricolored blackbird breeding foraging habitat must be planted in high- and very high-value crop types in any given year (see Appendix 13B, Section 13B.85.5.3, Table 13B.85-1, for definitions of foraging habitat values).
CMP-22b.rationale: Annual crop-mix threshold compliance by land managers.

CMP-22b.name: Prioritize Foraging Habitat Sites by Landscape Characteristics
CMP-22b.quote: Foraging habitat protection will be prioritized based on the following characteristics. Large contiguous landscapes that consist of high- or very high-value  cultivated lands, grasslands, vernal pool complex, and alkali seasonal wetland complex. Cultivated lands that incorporate riparian corridors, water conveyance  channels, grasslands, and wetlands. Cultivated lands that provide opportunities to maintain a mosaic of crop types  and allow for the periodic rotation of essential crop types (those crop types with very high, high, and moderate foraging habitat values) to nonessential crop types to ensure acreage commitments. Cultivated lands that expand upon or provide connectivity between existing  conservation lands.
CMP-22b.rationale: Site selection applying listed landscape and crop-rotation criteria.

CMP-22b.name: Maintain Wildlife Habitat Patches on Protected Cultivated Lands
CMP-22b.quote: Small patches of important wildlife habitats associated with protected cultivated lands will be maintained, including isolated valley oak trees, trees and shrubs along field borders and roadsides, remnant groves, riparian corridors, water conveyance channels, grasslands, ponds, and wetlands.
CMP-22b.rationale: Ongoing land management retaining trees, hedgerows, riparian corridors, ponds, and wetlands.

CMP-22b.name: Minimize Insecticide Use During Spring Nesting Season
CMP-22b.quote: On cultivated lands managed as high- to very high-value foraging habitat for tricolored blackbirds, insecticide use will be minimized to the greatest extent practicable during the spring growing season until tricolored blackbird nestlings have fledged or it is documented that no nearby nesting is occurring. This is to ensure that an abundant insect prey population is available to support egg development and feeding of the young, as well as to minimize the risk of pesticide toxicity effects.
CMP-22b.rationale: Behavioral restriction on insecticide application until nestlings fledge or no nearby nesting is documented.

CMP-22b.name: Include Insecticide Restrictions in Site Protection Instruments
CMP-22b.quote: Site protection instruments developed to protect tricolored blackbird breeding foraging habitat would include site management and site use restrictions, including the application of insecticide, as described in Section 3F.4.2.2.
CMP-22b.rationale: Legal site protection instruments must include site management and use restrictions; deliverable is the executed instrument.

CMP-23.name: Restore Tidal Perennial Habitat for Construction Impacts
CMP-23.quote: Tidal perennial habitat (e.g., including consideration of shallow water habitat components consistent with agency/regulatory requirements) would be restored to mitigate for both temporary and permanent construction impacts.
CMP-23.rationale: Restoration crews restore tidal perennial habitat via levee breach/setback, grading, fill import, channel excavation, and revegetation.

CMP-23.name: Coordinate Tidal Restoration Siting with CDFW, USFWS, NMFS
CMP-23.quote: Tidal perennial habitat restoration site selection and design will occur in coordination
CMP-23.rationale: Regulatory staff coordinate site selection and design with resource agencies.

CMP-23.name: Develop Tidal Restoration Siting, Design, Performance Criteria
CMP-23.quote: Siting, design, and performance criteria for tidal perennial habitat restoration will be developed based on assessments of topography, local hydrodynamic conditions, and sediment transport.
CMP-23.rationale: Engineers develop siting, design, and performance criteria from topographic, hydrodynamic, and sediment assessments.

CMP-23.name: Form Technical Team to Prepare Restoration and Management Plans
CMP-23.quote: As necessary and reflecting permitting requirements, a collaborative technical team including DWR and fishery agency representatives will be formed to select the most biologically appropriate and cost-effective restoration sites, design the restoration plan, set performance criteria, and develop the restoration unit management plan for the sites.
CMP-23.rationale: Planners with agency representatives select sites, design the restoration plan, and develop the restoration unit management plan, as permitting requires.

CMP-24.name: Restore Channel Margin Habitat for Construction Impacts
CMP-24.quote: Channel margin habitat would be restored to mitigate construction impacts for both temporary and permanent impacts. Channel margin restoration will be accomplished by improving channel geometry and restoring riparian, marsh, and mudflat habitats on the water side of levees along channels that provide rearing and outmigration habitat for juvenile salmonids in particular, similar to what is currently done by the USACE and others when implementing levee improvements.
CMP-24.rationale: Restoration crews improve channel geometry and restore riparian, marsh, and mudflat habitat on waterside of levees.

CMP-24.name: Design Restoration on Waterward Benches Maintaining Flood Conveyance
CMP-24.quote: Channel margin restoration associated with federal project levees will not be implemented on the levee, but rather on benches to the waterward side of such levees, and flood conveyance will be maintained as designed.
CMP-24.rationale: Engineers design restoration on waterward benches, not the levee, preserving flood conveyance.

CMP-24.name: Obtain USACE Section 408 Permission and NMFS/CDFW Site Approval
CMP-24.quote: Channel margin enhancements associated with federal project levees may require permission from USACE in accordance with USACE's authority under the Rivers and Harbors Act (33 USC § 408) and USACE levee vegetation policy. Sites for channel margin restoration will be subject to approval by NMFS and CDFW.
CMP-24.rationale: Permitting staff obtain USACE 408 permission where needed and NMFS/CDFW site approval.

CMP-24.name: Form Technical Team to Prepare Channel Margin Restoration Plan
CMP-24.quote: As necessary and reflecting permitting requirements, a collaborative technical team including DWR and fishery agency representatives will be formed to identify the most biologically appropriate and cost-effective restoration sites, design the restoration plan, set performance criteria, and develop the restoration unit management plan for the sites for DWR’s selection.
CMP-24.rationale: Planners with agency representatives identify sites, design the plan, set performance criteria, and develop the management plan, as permitting requires.

CMP-25.name: Undertake North Delta Tidal Habitat Restoration for Salmon
CMP-25.quote: DWR will undertake tidal habitat restoration in the north Delta to mitigate for potential hydrodynamics-related effects such as a greater frequency of Sacramento River reverse flows below Georgiana Slough compared to existing conditions, as reflected in the results of the hydrodynamic analyses and through-Delta juvenile Chinook salmon survival modeling.
CMP-25.rationale: Restoration crews implement tidal restoration offsetting operational hydrodynamic effects on juvenile Chinook.

CMP-25.name: Determine Tidal Restoration Extent with CDFW, NMFS, FWS
CMP-25.quote: The extent of this tidal habitat restoration will be determined in coordination with CDFW, NMFS, and FWS and in consideration of the following factors.
CMP-25.rationale: Analysts determine restoration extent considering other restoration, the Georgiana Slough barrier, and sea level rise/climate change, in coordination with agencies.

CMP-25.name: Monitor North Delta Mitigation Performance via Adaptive Management
CMP-25.quote: A monitoring program will be included to assess the performance of the mitigation and modify the mitigation approach as necessary through the Adaptive Management Program to offset the effects of the project alternatives as they become better understood.
CMP-25.rationale: Monitoring program assesses mitigation performance and feeds the Adaptive Management Program.

CMP-26.name: Restore Channel Margin Habitat for Operations Impacts on Salmon
CMP-26.quote: DWR will undertake channel margin habitat restoration to mitigate for potential flow-related impacts on riparian and wetland bench habitat used by juvenile Chinook salmon for rearing.
CMP-26.rationale: Restoration crews restore channel margin bench habitat (extent already calculated as total length of deficit), additional to construction mitigation. Calculation and efficacy text is context.

CMP-27.name: Restore Tidal Habitat for Delta Smelt in North Delta Arc
CMP-27.quote: DWR will mitigate potential project-related impacts on delta smelt by restoring tidal habitat, concentrated within the north Delta Arc or other areas deemed appropriate through consultation with USFWS and CDFW.
CMP-27.rationale: Restoration crews restore tidal habitat in the north Delta Arc or agency-agreed areas.

CMP-27.name: Monitor Delta Smelt Mitigation Effectiveness Long Term
CMP-27.quote: This mitigation measure’s effectiveness will be subject to long-term monitoring
CMP-27.rationale: Long-term effectiveness monitoring assessed with USFWS and CDFW under the Adaptive Management Program.

CMP-28.name: Restore Tidal Habitat for Longfin Smelt Flow Impacts
CMP-28.quote: DWR will undertake tidal habitat restoration to mitigate for potential flow-related impacts on longfin smelt.
CMP-28.rationale: Restoration crews restore tidal habitat sized by the Kratville (2010) method.

CMP-28.name: Obtain USFWS/CDFW Concurrence to Credit Construction Restoration
CMP-28.quote: With the concurrence of USFWS and CDFW, this habitat restoration mitigation requirement may be partly or fully met by tidal perennial or shallow water habitat restoration for construction effects.
CMP-28.rationale: Regulatory staff seek agency concurrence if construction-effects restoration is to satisfy this requirement.

CMP-29.name: Offset Crotch Bumble Bee Habitat Impacts
CMP-29.quote: Impacts on Crotch bumble bees and their habitat will be offset either through creation or enhancement of suitable habitat, land preservation through site protection instruments, the purchase of credits through a CDFW-approved mitigation bank, or the creation of non-bank site approved by CDFW.
CMP-29.rationale: Mitigation specialists offset impacts via habitat creation/enhancement, site protection, bank credits, or CDFW-approved non-bank site.

CMP-29.name: Include Nesting and Overwintering Features at CBB Mitigation Sites
CMP-29.quote: Mitigation sites will include flower rich natural habitats, grassland, and scrub habitats that include underground cavities (e.g., animal burrows) for nesting and overwintering and aboveground undisturbed areas with nesting resources, such as leaf litter or other complex habitat such as wood piles, tufts of grass, or rock walls for additional overwintering habitat (Xerces Society et al. 2018).
CMP-29.rationale: Site design criteria: floral resources, underground cavities, and aboveground nesting/overwintering features.

CMP-29.name: Include Insecticide Restrictions in CBB Site Protection Instruments
CMP-29.quote: Site protection instruments developed to protect Crotch bumble bee habitat would include site management and site use restrictions, including the application of insecticides, as described in U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Guidance for Assessing Pesticide Risks to Bees (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 2014) (also see Section 3F.4.2.2).
CMP-29.rationale: Legal site protection instruments must carry management and insecticide use restrictions per EPA bee guidance.

CMP-29.name: Offset Unsuccessful Nest Relocation with Suitable Habitat
CMP-29.quote: To offset the unsuccessful relocation of a nest, as determined by a qualified biologist, suitable habitat will be created, enhanced, or protected, using the mitigation mechanisms described above.
CMP-29.rationale: Triggered only when a qualified biologist determines a nest relocation failed; habitat within a 1.8 km buffer of the lost nest.
